displayQuote: Academic Politics Are So Vicious Because the Stakes Are So Small

meta.title: Who really said "Academic Politics Are So Vicious Because the Stakes Are So Small"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Henry Kissinger. The line was already an anonymous academic joke in print by 1969 and is known as Sayre's Law; Kissinger was credited only from 1977.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Academic Politics Are So Vicious Because the Stakes Are So Small'?
meta.ogDescription: Kissinger repeated it, but did not coin it. In print unattributed by February 1969, and named for Columbia's Wallace Sayre from 1973 onward.

answer.label: Not Henry Kissinger — long known as Sayre’s Law
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ finds no evidence that Kissinger coined this: the earliest full statements in print — a February 1969 speech by Columbia philosopher Charles Frankel and a 1970 essay by Dwight Waldo — both present it as a joke already in circulation, with no author attached. The saying has been called Sayre’s Law since 1973, when Charles Issawi’s Issawi’s Laws of Social Motion and a December 1973 Wall Street Journal column independently credited Columbia’s Wallace S. Sayre — and Sayre’s colleague Herbert Kaufman confirmed that origin four years later, in an Autumn 1977 letter to PS — but no text written by Sayre himself has ever been produced; Kissinger enters the record only in an August 1977 magazine editorial.

source.excerpt: It used to be said of politics on the university campus that it was the worst of all kinds of politics because the stakes were so small. We should be able to take at least minor comfort, then, from the present situation in the educational world: The stakes today are not at all small.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ lays out seventeen dated citations and concludes that the 1969 and 1970 appearances point to no creator — “the words were anonymous” — while the Kissinger credit first appears in an August 1977 editorial in The New Republic.

Barry Popik’s 2004 posting to the American Dialect Society list ↗ reprints Herbert Kaufman’s Autumn 1977 letter to PS in full, correcting that editorial and giving Sayre’s own formulation: “The politics of the university are so intense because the stakes are so low.”
Wikiquote ↗ files the university-politics line in the Misattributed section of its Henry Kissinger page, alongside two unattributed variants from 1983 and 1990.

Samuel Johnson’s 1765 Preface to Shakespeare ↗ supplies the precursor QI opens with: scholarly subjects “of very small importance” that somehow produce invective “more eager and venomous” than any political hack’s.
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest direct evidence of a full version that Quote Investigator has located ↗, and note how Frankel introduces it: “It used to be said…” He is quoting a joke he expects the room to know, and he names no author. The popular wording — vicious, small stakes — is a later polish on the same thought, not a sentence anyone has traced to a first speaker.
source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted, because the wording has no identifiable author or first publication. The individual printings that carry it — Frankel’s 1969 convention speech, Issawi’s 1973 book, the 1973 and 1983 Wall Street Journal columns, Kaufman’s 1977 letter — are all post-1930 and remain with their respective authors and publishers, but the one-line proverb itself belongs to no traceable source. Only the 1765 Samuel Johnson precursor quoted above is unambiguously public domain.

author.name: Wallace S. Sayre
author.heading: Who was Wallace Sayre?
author.bio: Wallace Stanley Sayre (June 24, 1905 – May 18, 1972) was an American political scientist who moved to Columbia University in 1954 and held the Eaton Professorship of Public Administration there until his death; The New York Times considered him a leading authority on New York City government. With Herbert Kaufman he wrote the 815-page Governing New York City (1960), still the standard anatomy of the city’s political machinery. He is remembered far more widely, and far less accurately, for a one-line joke about faculty meetings that no one can prove he wrote down.

copyAttribution: "Academic politics are so vicious because the stakes are so small." — not Henry Kissinger. The saying was already an anonymous academic joke in print by February 1969, and has been known as Sayre's Law after Columbia political scientist Wallace S. Sayre (1905–1972) since 1973. Kissinger was first credited with it by a New Republic editorial in August 1977; he repeated the line but did not coin it. Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: How Kissinger got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a saying with more claimants than sources. Every name below has carried it in print; none of them can be shown to have said it first.

items.why: The Kissinger link begins with an unsigned editorial in the 20 & 27 August 1977 issue of The New Republic, which wrote that the republic of learning and letters “works by squabbling—especially bitter squabbling, Henry Kissinger used to say, because the stakes are so small.” Quote Investigator finds nothing earlier tying him to it ↗ — and the saying was already in print, authorless, in 1969 and 1970.

He did tell it. A 1 September 1983 Wall Street Journal item reported that, asked where he acquired his facility for political intrigue, Kissinger said he had learned it all as a college professor, adding that academic politics is so bitter precisely because the stakes are so small — transcribed by Barry Popik ↗. Wikipedia’s Sayre’s law entry ↗ quotes a 1997 Ashbrook Center speech transcript in which he went further: “I formulated the rule…”

Charles Issawi’s Issawi’s Laws of Social Motion (1973) credited Sayre, and the Wall Street Journal of 20 December 1973 called it Sayre’s Third Law. In the Autumn 1977 issue of PS, Herbert Kaufman — Sayre’s coauthor — wrote that he had first heard it from Sayre’s own lips more than a quarter of a century earlier and that “scores of people will verify my statement of its origin.” But no text by Sayre carrying the line has surfaced ↗.

Publisher William Jovanovich told a Senate committee in August 1972 that when someone asked Unruh why campus politics were so nasty, he replied, “Because the stakes are so low” — one of several rival credits in QI’s chronology ↗.

Ralph Keyes reports that, per the onetime editor of Wilson’s papers, Wilson often said the intensity of academic squabbles at Princeton tracked the “triviality” of the issue — and gives the verdict “an old academic saw that may have originated with Woodrow Wilson but was put in modern play by Wallace Sayre” in The Quote Verifier ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: No one has produced a document in which Kissinger, Sayre, Unruh or Wilson wrote this down first. The two earliest full versions in print, from 1969 and 1970, both introduce it as a joke everyone already knew — and the strongest claim of authorship remains Herbert Kaufman’s 1977 letter ↗ saying he heard it from Wallace Sayre decades before anyone printed it.

context.heading: Why the joke keeps changing owners
lead: The line is a small masterpiece of compression, and that is exactly why it has no birth certificate. Sayings that are this quotable travel by repetition, not by publication — and each retelling strips off whatever attribution it arrived with. By the time anyone thought to write it down, the two earliest printings Quote Investigator can find ↗ already treat it as common property: Charles Frankel opened with “It used to be said…” in February 1969, and Dwight Waldo called it “our little joke” in 1970.

Kissinger inherited the line the way famous people usually do — by being the most quotable person in the room it described. He had been a Harvard professor before he was a Secretary of State, so the joke fit him too well to resist, and he told it about himself: a September 1983 Wall Street Journal piece reported that when asked where he learned political intrigue, he said he had learned it all as a college professor. Herbert Kaufman had already written to correct the record in 1977 ↗, and was generous about it: he assumed Kissinger never meant to claim authorship, any more than Kaufman claimed Newton’s laws by quoting them.
context.detailsSummary: The other people this has been pinned on
detailsBody: Jesse Unruh. The California politician was credited in August 1972 Senate testimony by publisher William Jovanovich — asked why campus politics were so nasty, Unruh reportedly answered, “Because the stakes are so low” — and again in a 1979 Antioch Review essay, per Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗.

Woodrow Wilson. Ralph Keyes reports in The Quote Verifier that, according to the onetime editor of Wilson’s papers, Wilson often observed that the intensity of the academic squabbles he watched as president of Princeton was a function of the “triviality” of the issues — the sample text is online at the Library of Congress ↗.

Richard Neustadt, Courtney Brown, Laurence J. Peter, C. P. Snow, Daniel Patrick Moynihan. All have carried a version at one time or another; Peter published his as “Peter’s Theory of Professional Infighting” in a 1983 newspaper column, which is how a joke acquires a fifth owner.
context.pull: “One might infer from this that Dr. Kissinger originated the line.” — Herbert Kaufman, letter to the editor, PS, Autumn 1977

schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Henry Kissinger, who repeated the line but is not documented as its originator. The earliest printings, in 1969 and 1970, name no author; the saying has been credited to Wallace S. Sayre since 1973 and is known as Sayre's Law, but no text written by Sayre carrying it has ever been produced.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI documents the earliest direct evidence of a full statement as a February 1969 speech by Charles Frankel that gives no attribution; concludes the 1969 and 1970 citations point to no creator and the words were anonymous; the Kissinger credit first appears in an August 1977 New Republic editorial; Sayre linked in Issawi 1973 and the 20 December 1973 Wall Street Journal; Kaufman's Autumn 1977 PS letter; Jesse Unruh via Jovanovich's August 1972 Senate testimony; the 1765 Samuel Johnson precursor; Laurence J. Peter's 1983 column; Neustadt in 1992.

Wikiquote lists 'The reason that university politics is so vicious is that the stakes are so small' in the Misattributed section of the Henry Kissinger page, with unattributed variants from 1983 (John C. Carr) and 1990 (John I. Goodlad).

Wikipedia's Sayre's law article states Sayre was a US political scientist at Columbia (1905-1972); that the Wall Street Journal of 20 December 1973 quoted him; that Herbert Kaufman attested to Fred Shapiro that Sayre's usual wording was 'The politics of the university are so intense because the stakes are so low' and that he originated the quip by the early 1950s; and quotes a 1997 Ashbrook Center speech in which Kissinger said 'I formulated the rule that the intensity of academic politics and the bitterness of it is in inverse proportion to the importance of the subject they're discussing.'

Barry Popik's 29 September 2004 ADS-L posting reprints Herbert Kaufman's Autumn 1977 PS letter in full ('One might infer from this that Dr. Kissinger originated the line'; Sayre's formulation; 'I myself first heard it from his lips more than a quarter of a century ago') and cites the Wall Street Journal of 1 September 1983 reporting that Kissinger, asked where he acquired his facility for political intrigue, said he learned it all as a college professor and that academic politics is so bitter precisely because the stakes are so small.

Ralph Keyes's The Quote Verifier opens chapter one with 'ACADEMIC politics are so vicious precisely because the stakes are so small,' notes it is routinely attributed to Kissinger, cites Neustadt, Sayre, Issawi 1973, Kaufman's wording, Peter's 1979 book, and Woodrow Wilson via the onetime editor of Wilson's papers; verdict: 'An old academic saw that may have originated with Woodrow Wilson but was put in modern play by Wallace Sayre.'

Samuel Johnson's Preface to Shakespeare (1765) contains: 'It is not easy to discover from what cause the acrimony of a scholiast can naturally proceed. The subjects to be discussed by him are of very small importance... there is often found in commentaries a spontaneous strain of invective and contempt, more eager and venomous than is vented by the most furious controvertist in politicks.'

Wallace Stanley Sayre (June 24, 1905 - May 18, 1972) was an American political scientist who moved to Columbia University in 1954 as Eaton Professor of Public Administration until his death, coauthored the 815-page Governing New York City with Herbert Kaufman, and is the namesake of Sayre's law.
